title: feat: add render_lonboard() for lonboard maps
description:
Part of #278

[lonboard](https://developmentseed.org/lonboard/) draws hundreds of thousands to millions of geospatial features on the GPU from Arrow data. With the new `@render_lonboard`, return a `lonboard.Map`, one or more layers, or the data itself (a GeoPandas `GeoDataFrame`, a GeoArrow table, anything `lonboard.viz()` accepts) and get a map that:

- fills its card/container like other shinywidgets outputs, while respecting an explicit `Map(height=...)` or `output_widget(height=...)` (and keeping lonboard's 500px default where there's nothing to fill);
- shows lonboard's default controls (fullscreen, zoom/compass, scale);
- exposes map state to the app through `reactive_read()` (e.g., `view_state`, or a layer's `selected_index`), and can be restyled in place via `.widget` without re-sending the data.

Before this PR, lonboard under shinywidgets had several problems: `import shinywidgets` followed by `import lonboard` raised a `RuntimeError`, the default controls never appeared, maps in containers shorter than 500px were clipped, an explicit `Map(height=...)` was ignored, and returning a layer rendered nothing.

### Notes

- **Shared default controls.** lonboard constructs `Map`'s default controls once, at import time, and shares them across every Map, so they can't belong to a Shiny session (and the browser never received them). `as_widget()` now gives each Map its own copies, preserving their settings. Since lonboard builds those controls while it's still being imported, `init_shiny_widget()` now lets widgets constructed during that window through without a session. This exemption is narrow: it only applies while lonboard's `Map` class body is executing.
- **Sizing.** `Map.__init__()` sets `layout.height="100%"`, which our generic check mistook for a user-specified height (so maps never filled). The new `_LAYOUT_DEFAULTS["lonboard"]` handler corrects `fill`. lonboard's root is `min-height: 100%; height: 500px`, so it already grows into a definite-height container. A scoped `max-height: 100%` in `shinywidgets.css` keeps it from overflowing shorter ones. With no definite height to fill (e.g., `output_widget(fillable=False)`), the map keeps lonboard's 500px. When the user sets `Map(height=...)`, the widget container sizes to the map, so that height actually applies. The stylesheet also drops lonboard's notebook-oriented -5px top offset.
- **Measured in the browser** (before → after):

  | case | before | after |
  |---|---|---|
  | map in a 300px card (266px output) | 500px tall, clipped | 266px |
  | `Map(height=200)` in a 400px card | 366px (height ignored) | 200px |
  | `output_widget(height="300px")` | 500px, clipped | 300px |
  | `output_widget(fillable=False)` with no height | 500px | 500px |

  A map in a fillable card exactly matches the card body and tracks window resizes. In a non-filling page, a default output uses shinywidgets' usual 400px fill fallback.
- **Transport benchmark.** Time to first render (navigation to all points loaded), Chromium with GPU, one map, median of 3:

  | points | websocket payload | time to render |
  |---|---|---|
  | 10 | 4.8 MB | 0.80 s |
  | 10k | 5.1 MB | 0.85 s |
  | 100k | 7.2 MB | 0.94 s |
  | 1M | 26.1 MB | 1.71 s |

  - The 10-point row is essentially the fixed baseline: page load plus about 4.8 MB of lonboard's inline anywidget JS/CSS, which every Map carries. Relative to it, 1M points add about 0.9 s and 21 MB on localhost.
  - Base64 inflates the Parquet buffers by 33% (16.0 MB becomes 21.3 MB at 1M). Python-side serialization is about 0.14 s at 1M.
  - With software WebGL (headless/CI-like), 1M points takes about 15 s, almost entirely inside GL. So real-browser numbers are the ones above.
  - This PR makes no transport changes.
  - Suggested follow-up: the 4.8 MB ESM is re-sent with every Map render (including re-renders), so caching or deduplicating anywidget `_esm`/`_css` would help more than binary transport for small and medium datasets.
- A page with several lonboard maps logs a benign `luma.gl ... already been initialized` console error from lonboard's own bundles.

### Verification

- `make py-check-format`, `make pyright` (0 errors), `make test-unit` (199 passed, 1 xfailed, no skips). The new `tests/unit/test_lonboard.py` covers:
  - layer → Map coercion;
  - per-session control copies, including when lonboard is first imported during a render and for `session_lifetime()` Maps;
  - import order;
  - the renderer's input shapes (Map, layer list, Arrow table) and the missing-dependency error;
  - the sizing rules.
- Playwright `tests/playwright/render_lonboard` (5 passed):
  - renders with controls and no unexpected console errors;
  - fills a card, tracks window resizes, and respects explicit `Map`/output heights;
  - keeps 500px in a non-fillable output;
  - a `view_state` drag round-trips to Python;
  - re-rendering keeps exactly one live view per output.

  The existing `render_matplotlib_fill` and `render_maplibre` suites still pass.
- Unit tests also pass on Python 3.10 (which resolves lonboard 0.13.0) and 3.14 (lonboard 0.17.0).
- `examples/lonboard` runs. Smoke test with a 100k-point GeoDataFrame: `view_state` populates, clicking a point fills the "Clicked point" panel, color/radius restyle in place, and there are no console errors.

title: feat: datashader plots re-aggregate on zoom/pan via @render_holoviews
description:
> **Merge note:** this PR must merge **after #284** (geoviews). #284 and this PR both rewrite the `@render_holoviews` CHANGELOG bullet and docstring, so whoever merges second will see conflicts in `CHANGELOG.md` and `shinywidgets/_render_widget.py`. Resolve them as follows.
>
> CHANGELOG, use one combined bullet:
>
> ``* `@render_holoviews` for [HoloViews](https://holoviews.org), [hvPlot](https://hvplot.holoviz.org), and [geoviews](https://geoviews.org) objects, including [datashader](https://datashader.org)-rasterized plots, which re-aggregate as you zoom and pan (requires shiny >= 1.9). Add `.opts(responsive=True)` to make a plot fill its container. (#87, #250, #253, #278)``
>
> Docstring: take geoviews' wording (summary and "holoviews/hvplot/geoviews object") plus datashader's extra sentence.

`@render_holoviews` can now plot millions of points with [datashader](https://datashader.org) and still behave interactively. Use `df.hvplot.points("x", "y", rasterize=True)` or holoviews' `rasterize()`. When you zoom or pan, datashader re-runs on the server for just the visible region, and the sharper image replaces the old one. Only an image-sized aggregate is sent to the browser, never the points themselves. This matches what users get in a notebook, and a static `@render.image` of a datashader image can't do it.

Part of #278.

**Requires shiny >= 1.9 for the re-aggregation.** Holoviews handles zoom events in its own background asyncio task, outside Shiny's input -> flush cycle. Shiny 1.9 (unreleased; py-shiny main) sends widget messages published that way right away, because registering a `session.on_flush()`/`on_flushed()` callback now requests an output flush (posit-dev/py-shiny#1889). On older shiny the server re-aggregates but the new image only reaches the browser after some unrelated input, so zooming just magnifies the low-resolution image. This was originally stacked on #296, which worked around that in shinywidgets; #296 is closed in favor of requiring the newer shiny. The docstring, CHANGELOG, and example README state the requirement, and the Playwright tests skip on shiny < 1.9.

To exercise that path in CI now, `pyproject.toml` gains a `[tool.uv.sources]` entry that resolves shiny from py-shiny main (pinned to a commit in `uv.lock`). That affects only `uv lock`/`uv sync`, not the package's published `shiny>=` requirement, and it pulls in the htmltools and narwhals versions dev shiny needs.

**Follow-up to consider:** when the next shiny release ships, drop the `[tool.uv.sources]` entry and raise the `shiny>=` floor in `pyproject.toml` to that version. Beyond datashader, it's what makes any widget update from an `asyncio` task or thread reach the browser without a click (the fastplotlib, nglview, and live-map cases from #278), so the floor would be worth raising for shinywidgets as a whole, not just this renderer.

This PR adds:
- `examples/datashader`: 1M clustered points, a count/mean aggregation picker, and a colormap picker, in a filling card.
- Playwright tests that zoom in a real browser and check that re-aggregation reaches the page.
- A datashader mention in the `render_holoviews` docstring and CHANGELOG entry.
- `datashader` in the test/dev dependencies.

### Notes

- Tested path: `rasterize=True` with wheel zoom and drag-pan. holoviews' `datashade()` uses the same RangeXY stream mechanism, but it isn't covered by a test here, so the docs only promise rasterize.
- There's no `render_datashader`. Datashader doesn't produce widgets; you use it through holoviews/hvPlot, which `render_holoviews` already handles.
- Measured in headless Chromium with 200k points:
  - Wheel-zoom to re-aggregated image in the browser took about 0.7-0.8 s, mostly bokeh's and holoviews' debounces.
  - Over three zooms, the displayed image width went 9.33 -> 4.66 -> 2.33 -> 1.17, matching the server's aggregation range each time.
  - On shiny 1.6.0, the image never updated (waited 20 s+).
- In the example app (1M points), the first render takes about 1.7 s and zoom re-aggregation about 0.8 s. With `responsive=True` in a fillable page, the plot fills the card (output 868x621 at a 1200x800 viewport) and tracks resizes.
- Default (non-responsive) hvPlot plots keep their fixed 700x300 size. That's how `render_holoviews` already behaves, and this PR doesn't change it.
- Observed but not fixed here: after a re-render, `Bokeh.index` keeps the detached root views of earlier renders. DOM canvases don't pile up. The tests only look at views still in the page.

### Verification

- New Playwright tests (`tests/playwright/render_holoviews_datashader`):
  - Each check waits on a single live condition: the image the browser shows has the same x-extent as the server's latest aggregation, and it's either narrower than half the original width (after a wheel zoom) or shifted right by at least a fifth of its width (after a drag-pan).
  - Re-render 3x: views don't pile up, and zoom still re-aggregates on the replacement widget.
  - Both pass with py-shiny main (1.8.1.dev34) and unmodified shinywidgets `main` underneath. With shiny 1.6.0 from `uv.lock`, both time out waiting for the re-aggregated image, hence the version skip.
- With shiny from py-shiny main in `uv.lock`: `make py-check-format`, `make pyright`, `make test-unit` (182 passed), and the datashader Playwright tests pass. The full Playwright suite (70 tests) passes too.

title: fix: deliver widget updates made outside a reactive flush (background tasks, threads)
description:
Widget changes made outside Shiny's reactive cycle now reach the browser on their own. Before this PR they stayed queued until something else, typically an unrelated click or input change, triggered a Shiny flush. Affected changes include those made from an `asyncio` task, a timer, a frame-callback loop, or a background thread.

That stall made live and streaming widgets look broken:

- A fastplotlib canvas rendered at 0 fps.
- The final frame of a zoom gesture never arrived.
- A holoviews/datashader plot never showed its re-aggregated image after zooming. holoviews runs the re-aggregation from a debounced asyncio callback.
- nglview, which calls widget methods from its own thread, would stall the same way.

The root cause: Shiny for Python only flushes after client input, `invalidate_later()`, or an `ExtendedTask`, and shinywidgets queues every comm message on the session's flush callbacks.

Found while working on #278. The holoviews/datashader renderer PR is stacked on this one and relies on it.

### What changed

Whenever a widget message is queued, shinywidgets now also requests a flush. It does this the same way Shiny's own `invalidate_later()` and `ExtendedTask` do: `async with reactive.lock(): await reactive.flush()`.

### Notes

- **Ordering is unchanged.** Messages still go through `session.on_flush`/`on_flushed`. Children are opened before parent updates reference them, and an old widget is closed after its replacement renders.
- **Remaining ordering gap.** This gap existed before this PR and is now documented in the code. A child opened partway through a session's flush can trail its parent's update by one flush. That used to mean "until the next input"; it is now milliseconds.
- **No extra traffic for normal flushes.** Requested flushes are coalesced per session. A flush is skipped if one already in progress delivered the messages, so input-driven flushes add nothing.
- **Threads.** Calls from other threads are handed to the session's event loop with `call_soon_threadsafe`.
- **Off-loop sessions.** If a session's first widget was built off the loop, the loop is adopted on the first publish from the loop. It is also re-recorded at every session flush, so a loop captured from the wrong thread corrects itself.
- **Ended sessions.** Nothing is requested after a session ends.
- **Measured locally** (Chromium on one machine; two labels ticking every 100 ms with no input, over 5 s):
  - `main`: 0 updates arrived.
  - This branch: 49 updates from the asyncio task and 47 from the thread, with about 1 ms median and 2 ms max latency.
- **Cost.** `reactive.flush()` is global in py-shiny. So, like every `invalidate_later()` tick, each out-of-band flush also sends a small empty `values` message to every connected session. A real per-session `_request_flush` in py-shiny (today it's a no-op) would let this be narrowed later.

### Verification

- New unit tests in `tests/unit/test_comm_transport.py` drive a real Shiny session loop on a `MockConnection`. They cover:
  - delivery outside a flush
  - delivery from another thread
  - a message published late in a flush
  - no redundant flush when a flush already delivered the messages (the requested flush task is awaited)
  - lazy loop adoption
  - a cancelled flush request not blocking later ones
  - no flush after the session ends

  On `main`, the four delivery tests (outside a flush, from a thread, late in a flush, after the session ends) time out. The newer tests reference attributes that don't exist on `main`. The tests also pass when the file is run several times in one process, because Shiny's process-global reactive lock is reset per test.
- New Playwright test `tests/playwright/comm_outside_flush`: with no client input, updates from an asyncio task and from a thread reach the browser in order within the latency bound. It fails on `main` with 0 updates.
- The datashader zoom Playwright tests from the stacked PR pass on this branch and time out on `main`.
- The existing ordering and lifecycle Playwright suites pass (33 tests), including `ipyleaflet_layer_updates`, `container_child_views`, all `*_rerender_cleanup` suites, `cross_session`, `session_churn`, and `widget_lifetimes`.
- `make py-check-format`, `make pyright`, and `make test-unit` (189 passed) all pass.

title: fix: as_widget() raises a helpful TypeError for builtin values
description:
If a `@render_widget` (or any `render_*`) function accidentally returns a string, dict, number, or `object()`, users currently get `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute '__module__'`. That traceback points into shinywidgets internals and hides the helpful `TypeError("Don't know how to coerce ... into a ipywidget.Widget object.")` that `as_widget()` is meant to raise (including the `@render.ui` hint for objects with `_repr_html_`). With this change the intended error shows up.

Found while working on #278.

## Notes

- Cause: `widget_pkg()` did `w.__module__.split(".")[0]`. Classes and instances of user-defined classes have `__module__`, but instances of builtins don't.

Builtin instances now map to `"builtins"`, which matches nothing in `AS_WIDGET_MAP`, so `as_widget()` reaches its normal `TypeError`. Existing callers (classes via `type(x).__mro__`, widget instances, `_LAYOUT_DEFAULTS` lookup) are unchanged.
- No issue exists for this one; the changelog bullet references this PR.

## Verification

- New tests failed before the fix (`AttributeError`) and pass after: `as_widget()` on `"x"`, `1`, `1.5`, `None`, `{}`, `[]`, `(1, 2)`, `object()`; `widget_pkg()` on classes and builtin instances; and a render-level test where a render function returns a string.

title: feat: add render_nglview() for nglview molecular viewers
description:
> **Stacked on #300** (`fill-fixed-size-hook`), which adds the shared `setupFixedSize` widget-behavior hook. Review/merge #300 first; this PR's diff is against that branch.

Part of #278 (answers #57).

You can now put an interactive [nglview](https://nglviewer.org/nglview/latest/) molecular viewer in a Shiny app with `@render_nglview`: return an `nglview.NGLWidget` and it fills its card, tracks its container's size as that changes, and respects an explicit `output_widget(height=...)`. Picking an atom is available in Python via `reactive_read(view.widget, "picked")`.

### Notes

- nglview sizes its stage in fixed inline pixels and never re-measures its parent, so out of the box it did not follow its container's width (canvas stayed 874px in a 574px output) and overflowed an explicit height (300px canvas in a 250px output). Python/CSS can't fix that (the stage size is set from JS), so `fill.ts` gets an `nglview` behavior that drives the stage size from the output element (observing the output, not the widget, to avoid feedback; `js/src/nglview.ts`). It uses the shared hooks from #300: `setupFill` for a filling output, and `setupFixedSize` (a no-op unless the output has an explicit height) otherwise. Cleanup and the default post-display resize come from the output binding. Measured after: canvas matches the output exactly at 874x398, and at 574x398 after narrowing; 876x250 for `height="250px"`.
- nglview's JS loads through the existing require/nbextension path (served locally, no CDN, no console errors).
- No coercion is needed: `NGLWidget` is already a widget.
- `nglview` is sdist-only on PyPI (it builds fine on Python 3.10-3.14) and brings in `notebook`/`jupyterlab`, hence the large `uv.lock` diff.
- nglview's post-load method calls (`add_representation`, ...) run on its own thread and were delivered one reactive flush late; that is addressed by the separate core PR "fix: deliver comm messages published outside a reactive flush" (branch `fix-comm-outside-flush`). title: Add a setupFixedSize widget behavior hook for outputs with their own size
description:
## Why

Several of the new `@render_*` PRs wrap widgets that size themselves from a fixed pixel value and ignore their container. To make them follow the output's size, they need JS help in two situations:

- the output **fills** its layout. `WidgetBehavior.setupFill()` already covers this.
- the output **has a size of its own** but isn't filling, e.g. `output_widget(height="500px")`. Nothing covers this yet.

Without a shared hook, each PR invented its own mechanism for the second case: a new `setupFixedSize` hook, a `fill` flag on `BehaviorContext`, and sniffing the `forward-fill-potential` class in `onDisplayed`. The last one is subtly wrong because that class is never removed. A fourth PR had no mechanism at all, so its plots stayed at the default height inside a taller output. The three mechanisms also conflict with each other textually in `fill.ts`/`output.ts`.

This PR settles on one hook that all of them build on: an optional `WidgetBehavior.setupFixedSize()`. The output binding runs it **instead of** `setupFill()` when the render isn't filling. It gets the same "only if this view is still current" guard and the same cleanup-on-view-removal wiring.

It also fixes a related core bug. The `forward-fill-potential` class, whose CSS stretches the widget to fill the output, was only ever added and never removed. After an output rendered one filling widget, every later widget rendered into it was stretched to fill as well, even when the server had decided it shouldn't fill (e.g., a widget with `layout.height="200px"`). The class now follows each render's fill decision.

## Impact

- The hook does nothing on its own: no widget behavior registers `setupFixedSize` yet.
- The class fix is user-visible. A re-render that goes from filling to not filling now takes its own size (200px, not the container's 400px). There's a CHANGELOG bug-fix bullet.
- Tests:
  - New generic Playwright regression test (`fill_to_fixed_rerender`). It uses a plain `ipywidgets.Output`, so it needs no optional packages. It failed before the fix (400 != 200) and passes after.
  - The full Playwright suite (69 tests) and the unit tests pass.

## Stacked PRs

These are rebased onto this branch and use the hook:

- #286 `@render_quak`: lifts quak's row cap for a filling or explicitly sized output.
- #290 `@render_nglview`: sizes the stage from the output.
- #292 `@render_keplergl`: drives the `height` trait from the output.

title: feat: add render_plotnine() for plotnine via ipympl
description:
Part of #278.

plotnine users can now use `@render_plotnine` to get an interactive [ipympl](https://matplotlib.org/ipympl/) widget instead of a static image. They can:

- zoom and pan from the toolbar.
- use matplotlib event callbacks (clicking a point, key presses, selectors). These run in Python and can update the figure in place without losing the current zoom.
- use a plot that fills its card in filling layouts and follows it as it resizes. plotnine re-lays out the legend, axis labels and titles at every size.
- render plot compositions like `(p1 | p2) / p3`.

`@render_widget` and `@render_matplotlib` now accept ggplot objects too. A new example app (`examples/plotnine/`) shows click-to-inspect with an in-place highlight, and a composition that fills its card.

```python
@render_plotnine
def plot():
    return ggplot(penguins, aes("flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g", color="species")) + geom_point()
```

### Notes

- **The returned plot isn't modified.** Each render draws a copy, as plotnine's own `save()` and `show()` do. Without the copy, `draw()` attaches the figure to the plot and the next render reuses it. Re-rendering the same ggplot or composition gives independent figures.
- **No pyplot leaks.** plotnine closes its pyplot figure after drawing. 25 render/retire cycles leave `plt.get_fignums()` unchanged.
- **Re-layout on resize.** plotnine's layout engine runs on every draw, so ipympl's fill-resize re-lays out the plot. Measured in the browser at 1000x800, 800x1000 and 1400x500 viewports: the canvas matches its card within 1px (e.g. 859x347), the Python figure is the same size, and no text is clipped.
- **Explicit heights.** In filling layouts the container sets the size and overrides `theme(figure_size=...)`, the same way `@render_matplotlib` overrides `figsize`. With an explicit output `height`, the figure is *not* fitted to the output, so set `figure_size` to match; the default 640x480 figure gets clipped by a smaller output. With `fill=False` and no height, the figure's width still follows its container. This is existing ipympl behavior shared with `@render_matplotlib`. A possible follow-up: an explicit output height should size the ipympl figure for both `render_matplotlib` and `render_plotnine`.
- **Open question: hiding the header.** ipympl normally labels the canvas "Figure N". plotnine frees its pyplot figure number right after drawing, so every plot would show a meaningless "Figure 1". The header is hidden for plotnine plots only; `@render_matplotlib` still shows it. Is that inconsistency OK, or should both behave the same?

### Verification

  - the hidden header
